summary: Defines the second version of the Remote Network Monitoring MIB, which lets network monitoring devices report on traffic seen on a network. It extends monitoring beyond the link layer to higher protocols. It was replaced by RFC 4502.

eli5.summary: A little watcher sits on the network and writes down what goes by. Managers can ask the watcher for its notes.

what is the difference between rmon and rmon2
subtitle: The second generation of remote network monitoring: probes that report traffic by protocol, all the way up to the application layer.

tldr.problem: Network managers needed monitoring probes that could tell them more than link-level counts, including which protocols and which hosts were generating traffic.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2021 defines the RMON2 MIB, a set of SNMP objects arranged in nine groups that let a probe decode protocols above the link layer, count traffic per address and per conversation, and keep history on the probe itself.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4502, which is the version to read today.

today: RFC 2021 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4502, so new work should use that document. It extended the original RMON MIB of RFC 1757.

sections.title: What RMON2 Adds
sections.content:
This memo continues the architecture of the original RMON MIB (RFC 1757) with what it calls a major feature upgrade, mainly analysis of traffic up to the application layer. It is a MIB, a set of objects that an SNMP agent exposes, for managing remote network monitoring devices, often called monitors or probes.

Probes are instruments that exist to manage a network. An organization may use one per network segment, and a service provider may use them to reach a remote client network. The objects are meant as an interface between an RMON agent and a management application, not for people to type in by hand.
sections.eli5: RMON2 teaches the little network watcher to notice not just that something passed by, but what kind of thing it was.

sections.title: Goals and the Nine Groups
sections.content:
The RFC lists five goals: offline operation (a probe keeps collecting statistics even when the management station cannot reach it), proactive monitoring (logging performance so history is available when a failure starts), problem detection and reporting, value added data (such as highlighting the hosts that generate the most traffic or errors) and support for multiple managers.

The objects are arranged into nine groups: protocol directory, protocol distribution, address mapping, network layer host, network layer matrix, application layer host, application layer matrix, user history, and probe configuration. The groups are the basic units of conformance: a device that implements a group must implement every object in it. Implementations must also implement the system and interfaces groups of MIB-II.

The memo also enhances tables from RMON. It adds the DroppedFrames and LastCreateTime conventions to each RMON table, lets filters match at an offset from the start of a protocol even when its headers vary in length, and defines extra filter and capture status bits for WAN and generic media.
sections.eli5: The watcher keeps its notes in nine separate notebooks, such as one for kinds of traffic and one for who talks to whom. If it keeps a notebook, it has to fill in every page.

sections.title: Sharing a Probe Among Managers
sections.content:
Many groups pair a read/write control table, where a manager sets parameters, with a read-only data table that holds the results. Most parameters can change only while the control entry is not active, so a manager deactivates the entry, changes it and reactivates it. Deleting a control entry also deletes its data entries, which frees the resources.

Because probe memory and computation are scarce, every manager-initiated function carries an OwnerString label naming who set it up. This lets a manager recognize its own leftover rows, lets an operator find who owns a resource, and lets an operator free resources that a crashed station never released. Resources that belong to the device or its administrator use an owner string starting with monitor, and managers should change those only under the administrator's direction. A manager is encouraged to scan a control table for a similar instance to share before creating a new one.

New rows are created with the RowStatus method from RFC 1903. If two managers try to create the same row at once, only the first succeeds and the others get an error. The RFC advises agents to check parameters as each object is set, rather than only when the row goes active, so the manager learns which value was bad.
sections.eli5: Many people may want to use the same watcher, so each one writes their name on what they ask for. That way nobody grabs the same notebook at once, and abandoned requests can be cleaned up.

sections.title: Protocol Directory and Counting Rules
sections.content:
Every RMON2 implementation can parse certain packet types and identify the protocol at several levels. The protocol directory is the inventory of protocols the probe can monitor, and it allows entries to be added, deleted and configured. Protocols are found by static software written at implementation time, so a probe cannot suddenly learn a new packet type. It does allow limited extensibility: if the code already knows where the demultiplexing field is, decoding of the next layer up can be table-driven, but no more than one level higher. The RFC's example is a probe that recognizes UDP ports 161 as SNMP, 53 as DNS and 69 as TFTP, and that an SNMP operation could extend to count UDP port 123 as NTP.

The term application level does not mean OSI layer 7 only. It covers any protocol above the MAC and network layers, including transport, session, presentation and application protocols.

Packets with link-level errors are not counted anywhere in this MIB. Packets with a protocol error are counted for all protocols below the layer where the error was found, so a network-layer error means the packet is not counted at all.
sections.eli5: The watcher has a list of the kinds of mail it knows how to read. Someone can add one more kind to the list, but only if the watcher already knows roughly how to open that envelope.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
To implement this MIB, a probe must capture all packets on its local network, including packets between third parties, and analyze them to collect addresses, protocol usage and conversation statistics. That data may be sensitive in some environments, so administrators may want to restrict SNMP access to the probe.

A probe that implements this MIB is likely to implement RMON (RFC 1757) too, which can return the contents of captured packets, possibly including user data or passwords. The RFC recommends restricting SNMP access to those functions.
sections.eli5: A watcher that sees everything going by also sees private things. So you should only let trusted people ask it questions.

sections.title: User History and the TimeFilter Appendix
sections.content:
The user history group lets a manager choose which MIB instances to sample, then has the probe collect them into buckets. This task was traditionally done by management applications through periodic polling, and the group lets it be offloaded to the probe.

The TimeFilter textual convention lets an application download only the rows that changed since a particular time. An appendix gives implementation notes for it. The RFC's definitions section also covers the probe configuration group, which controls operating parameters of the probe.
sections.eli5: Instead of a manager asking again and again, the watcher can keep its own diary of the numbers the manager picked and hand over only the new pages.
